scores.why: Today's page is the glow-rich original, but it is a wash of one green on black, and the owner has said it is too bright and too monochrome.
Desk Terminal puts the glass in a left column and adds a teal ground and a Coming up rail, a real change across the page, though the left column feels crowded.
Track Diagram has the Signal Box line language the owner loved on Home, To do and Chat (the thread hangs from Vera), with section colours and a monitor that still glows.
Tallied Gauge is calm and matte with an oscilloscope that really glows, but it reads as a tidy table page, with less line art and less personality.
Blueprint is a distinct drafting-sheet idea with fine grid lines, a title block and tinted idea hatching, which the owner would see on every page; the scalloped bubbles and heavy frame risk clutter.

Grid Console has fine rails with nodes and a NOW marker that draw the eye through the whole page, serif heads, grounded section colours and a glowing monitor; it is the closest to the Flight Deck and Signal Box taste.
Swiss Thread is calm, modern and well typeset with a good three-column home, but its CRT soul sits only in the monitor and the lit word.
The early Desk Terminal is a competent bar to measure against, but it is the least changed of the carried designs and has the thinnest line language.
Folding the glass to a Ready line takes away the monitors and the phosphor glow the owner values, and the slate change is too quiet to make up for it.
The spend dial and the heavy lead words are good instrument touches, but the page looks nearly the same as its parent, and the dial is off-screen on Home.
This keeps Track Diagram's spine and thread, and the faint runner and status line help; the change is subtle but the base is strong.
Thin section-coloured caps on every tray and squarer boxes show up on every page and sharpen the structure with no extra glare.
The dated To do spine and the small-caps labels add real typographic order, but the Home is still the plain tallied tables.
Tally ticks and rule caps add parts the family would not use, which fails the simplicity test; the mixed grammar of ticks and numerals is clumsy.
Cream ink and sage on the Blueprint are a nice material change, but the running head repeats the title and bar.
The pilot lamp on the title block and the quiet row of links are tidy but small refinements to a good base.
Grid Console with a counted head and a proper UP pilot lamp in the foot gives the line art an end point, and the lamp key is calmer; a fine child of the leader.
Dotted ledger leaders and the phosphor halo on the lead words of live rows bring back the lit-tube DNA where the rows are live, on top of the best structure in the field.
Serif headings on Swiss Thread are elegant but fall away from the CRT feel, and the thin current-page rule is a small gesture.
Raised select keys and true small caps add craft to the Swiss base, but a fourth face is added and the change is hard to see on Home.

Lit Index is the boldest idea: a giant condensed question with a raster-lined glowing word, a numbered index as navigation and big figures; it restores the glow strongly, but it is very long and the lit word reads olive.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the dotted leaders and the lead-word halo, since the glow sits on live rows only. Make the halo visible at card size, and carry the rail and NOW language into the Plans and To do pages too.
Keep the rails, nodes and serif heads. Calm the second NOW clock on Home, and make the cards' amber, violet and pink edges quieter and fewer so the page does not look like a rainbow of tabs.

Keep the giant lit word with its raster lines and the numbered index. Shorten the page (smaller index names, tighter rows), lift the deep green so it reads as phosphor, and size the type steps so Chat and Ideas feel like the same family.

Keep the thin drafting lines, the hatched idea kinds and the sheet grid, which are a lot of the line art the owner likes. Soften the scalloped bubbles, shrink the title-block frame, and make the grid fainter.
Keep the teal-black and slate plate colours, but do not fold the glass: Next up and the radar are the motif and must stay on first view.
Keep the rule with an end cap on the section head, which is simple and clear. Drop the tally ticks, which add a second way to say the count.
Keep the Home tracks and the Chat thread. Add the same line language to the Plans and Settings pages, and put the serif count on the Ideas head only when it earns its place.

judges.notes: The field splits in three. The Desk Terminal and Tallied lines (head-1, head-3, mut-1, mut-2, mut-5, mut-6) are the least changed and the most like each other; the owner has said "nearly identical" is the fault, and their child changes (a dial, ticks, a fold) are small or cost the monitors. The Swiss Thread line is calm and well typeset, but its CRT soul lives only in the monitor. The track and rail line (head-2, head-5 and their children) is the strongest: lines that delimit areas and lead the eye, serif heads, grounded colours and a glowing glass, which is what the owner praised in Signal Box and Flight Deck. Of those, mut-10 is the best because it brings back the lit-word halo and dotted ledger leaders where the data is live, so the page keeps the original's glow without glare. The Blueprint line and the wild Lit Index are the new ideas most worth developing: Blueprint for fine-line drafting structure on every page, Lit Index for a scanline-lit hero word that really recovers the original look. The yardstick 00-current is scored low because it is still one green on black.

parts.what: Monitor in a thin bezel with scan-lit radar, Next up and a typed line, set on a bloom; the scope with a trace is the runner
To do as a dated spine: a left Due margin, nodes on a rail and a lit NOW; the runner is the day-numeral cards with a NOW tick
Thread hung from Vera's mark on a rail with times in the margin and a ring at the composer
Teal-black ground with grounded section hues (amber, steel blue, mauve) as thin edges; cool slate with cream text as the runner
Serif page titles over mono small labels and a grotesque body; the runner is the condensed display with a lit word
Raster-lined bloom on the key word and the primary key; the runner is a two-layer halo on live lead words only

scores.why: The original tube light is all here (halo on the key word, real green monitors, scanlines), but it is a wash of near-monochrome green with little else lit meaningfully.
Vera's question, Next up, radar, trend scope and spend all live inside real VT323 green tubes on grounded slate, with lamp-row status dots; the light is concentrated and the page around it calmer.
Serif heads and counts make a handsome calm page, but the phosphor shows only in the Next up tube and one glowing word; the rest has gone matte.
The scope with its vertical sweep line and plan bars is a good live tube, but the page head and status are plain and the tube is the only lit thing.
Drafting-sheet frame with a bezelled dashed tube, bloom and a hatched afterglow card keeps real CRT light on a calm sheet; the headers are cooler than lit.
The tube has a perspective floor grid, Vera's greeting glows and the nav is lit, so the console feels like a powered machine, though the serif title is dim.
A big haloed word and a glowing Add key plus a real tube bring back the bloom boldly, but the layout is a flat Swiss page and the bloom bleeds.
Typed VT323 question inside the tube, radar, and a true moving-coil dial on the glass: the most unmistakably 1980s of the carried set.
Folding the glass to a READY line is a charming pilot-light idea, but it removes the radar, Next up and spend monitors that are the soul of the page.
Desk Terminal's lit tubes plus a phosphor moving-coil spend dial on Status: data drawn as light on a real screen, everything else matte and grounded.
Essentially the Counted Folio again; the runner banding is a quiet to-do refinement and does not bring any glow back.
Same calm serif page with section caps; the press afterglow only exists when pressed, so the tube light is no stronger than the parent.
The scope tube is alive and the lit NOW lamp on the To do spine is a good phosphor signal, but the rest is steel and condensed type.
Tally ticks and the masthead rule are matte and counted by intent; the tube is unchanged, so the soul rests on one monitor.
Cream ink and sage on a teal-black sheet beside a bezelled lit tube with a status line; warm and material, with the glow kept to the monitor and the key word.
As Cream Ink with a white-hot pilot lamp on the title block and a breathing glass lamp, small living lights in the right places.
Lit nav, haloed Vera, floor-gridded tube and a pilot lamp keep the console powered; the steel/pewter lamp key is grounded but dims the lamp language.
Console with a fuller dial and a halo on the lead words of live rows, which carries the tube's light into the lists exactly where the NOW marker sits.
Serif headings with a glowing Add key and a lit single letter; handsome, but the serif and the flat black page trade away the screen feel.
Same Swiss page, with a haloed MIND, a bright Add key and true small caps; the bloom is back but the surrounding page is a plain dark sheet.

A giant raster-scanned phosphor word, a beige 1980s monitor casing, lit numbered index and warm paper-white names: the boldest return of the tube's bloom and scanlines across the page, with tasteful companions.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the scanlined glowing key word, the beige monitor casing and the lit numbered index; lighten the green a touch so the raster lines don't read olive, cut the home height and set the index names a size down so the glow stays scarce.
Keep the dial drawn as light on the Status tube and the light numerals; make fig lines more even beside text and add the lit sector from mut-10 so the dial moves as it spends.
Keep the lit sector with the LIMIT flag and the halo on live lead words; strengthen the lead-word halo to a visible lit word at 100%, and give the spend dial a demo value so it shows.
Keep the single READY line as a pilot light, but fold only when truly idle on secondary pages; leave Home's Next up, radar and spend tubes open since those are the motif.
Keep the tube-led Home and lamp-row status; give the lists below a touch of the lead-word halo so the light continues past the tube.

judges.notes: The soul test favours designs where the page content carries the tube: Vera's question, Next up, radar, trend and spend drawn as light on real screens, with matte grounded plates elsewhere. Wild-1 is the boldest return of the original's bloom and scanlines, and mut-2 and head-1 do it most coherently. The Track Diagram and Tallied families are calm and well typeset but keep the phosphor to one tube, and the Swiss pair brings the glow back on one word and a key over a plain dark page. Folding the glass (mut-1) is a clever idea that gives up the monitors the owner likes.

parts.what: scanlined glowing key word with a two-layer halo; lead-word halo on live list rows
Vera's typed question, Next up and trend or dial all in one VT323 tube with a cursor
giant condensed title with folio number and rule under it; or serif title with a typed count
lamp-row status dots (lit and hollow) with dotted leaders; white-hot pilot lamp on the title block
moving-coil spend dial drawn in phosphor on the Status tube

scores.why: Strong signature but monochrome green on black, the Matrix feeling; one note of colour and little typographic play.
Teal ground, cream words and a tube column are a clear step from today, but it is a sober dashboard with no big idea.
Desk Terminal with the green tube as a left sidebar and a numbered, ruled, coloured-cap column reads as one considered system; handsome but familiar by now.
Serif display headings with purple counted numerals and a dated spine give it an editorial voice, and the vertical chat thread is lovely; it is a little busy with accent colours.
Tidy and legible, with a distinct scope trace for plans, but the rest is a competent admin dashboard with no strong personality.
The drafting-sheet Blueprint has a real identity (title blocks, grid margins, hatched swatches, scalloped bubbles) and the family would remember it, but it leans costume and is dense.
A lit thread running down the page with node dots, serif titles and a NOW stamp gives it a confident machine-and-print character; the glow is used with discipline.
Inter with a numbered nav, big thin 01/02 numerals and blue date figures is clean and distinct; it feels Swiss rather than phosphor, and the glow is mostly confined to the tube.
Slate plates and light numerals are tasteful, but folding the tube to one READY line takes away the monitors that carry the motif.
A moving-coil spend dial and heavy first words add instrument feel, but the dial sits on Status and Home is barely different from its parent.
The alternating runner on the dated To do spine and the status line under the chat question are neat details of a good system, but they are quiet.
Section-coloured caps on every tray add colour variety across pages and the squarer boxes read crisper; the press afterglow is invisible in stills.
The To do timetable spine with a lit NOW and true small caps is a good idea, but Home is almost unchanged from its parent.
Tick-mark counts and end-capped rules give a ledger feel, but the grammar is mixed (ticks beside numerals) and the overall look stays matte and generic.
Warm cream ink with sage and cyan companions on the blueprint's teal-black sheet is the most pleasing palette in the field, and the running head adds a bookish rhythm.
The pilot lamp on the title block and the dotted view links are fine touches, but the change is small and mostly in the footer.
A typed count on the Ideas head rule, a pilot lamp in the foot and steel and pewter lamp states make the console feel like a calm instrument panel with a clear voice.
Phosphor halo on the lead words of each row and dotted ledger leaders bring the original lit-tube effect onto the page content while keeping the calm console structure.
Serif headings over mono labels with a green lit word make the Swiss layout feel printed and warm, and the effect shows on every page; it is unusual for this field and elegant.
Condensed small-cap labels and raised keys are good typesetting, but the Swiss layout is otherwise unchanged and a fourth face is added.

A poster-like Home with a huge condensed question, a lit word with raster lines and halo, and a numbered index as navigation is the boldest and most memorable identity, and it restores the original phosphor glow where it belongs; the home is long and the lit word can read olive.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the giant condensed question, lit word and numbered index; shorten Home by making each index row's name smaller beside short rows, and lift the lit word's green a little so it reads as glowing rather than olive.

Keep the lit lead words and dotted leaders; make the halo a touch stronger at half size and apply it consistently to the plan and idea titles, so the original phosphor effect is clearly seen on content.
Keep the cream ink with sage and cyan; give the running head something the bar does not already say (a date or a count) so it is not redundant.
Keep the typed count and pilot lamp; fix the Status head's empty space above the title and drop the lamp key row that adds words.
Keep the serif headings with the lit green word; make the current-page rule thicker or brighter so it reads, and carry the serif into section heads on Plans and To do.
Keep the slate plates and light numerals but never fold the tube; leave the Next up readout and radar visible and fold only the idle status text.

judges.notes: The field is crowded with near-twins: five carried families (Desk Terminal, Track Diagram, Tallied, Blueprint, Grid Console) plus two Swiss, and most children change one corner or one label, which the owner has said they do not want. Only a few change the page's character across all pages. Lit Index is the one clean-sheet idea, and it does what the owner asked in the last word: it brings back the original tube's bloom and halo on the words that matter, and makes the type the identity. Its cost is length and a slightly muddy lit word. Ledger Dial shows how the old glow can return on row lead words without losing the calm. Cream Ink is the best colour work, and Serif Swiss Thread shows a small type change that reaches every heading. The Tallied children are clean but timid. The Desk Terminal folds hide the monitors, which is the wrong trade.

parts.what: folio plus one giant condensed word with the lede on its baseline; or a typed count standing on the masthead rule
tube with a scope trace of plans as pulses and a NOW marker, with a mono status line on the glass
wide-range condensed display with a lit key word over small mono labels; or serif headings over mono labels
warm cream ink and sage and cyan companions on a teal-black ground; or blue-grey slate plates
ruled section heads with coloured ends, hatched kind swatches and a title block; or a lit thread with nodes
title-block footer (project, motto, drawn, sheet) with a pilot lamp on its top rule; or a pilot lamp in the console foot

scores.why: Clear enough and the composer is reachable, but monochrome green, ungrouped labels and a thin hierarchy; the yardstick.
Tube first, then composer, with small-caps FROM labels and a real select list; coherent but the tube pushes the box below the glass and it is close to its siblings.
One Vera card holds greeting, question, a Listening status line and the composer, so title, then action, then content reads cleanly; select list and focus rings are clear.
Condensed question with a READY line and a clear Send; solid, but the native highlighted select row breaks the system and it is a quiet change.
Drafted sheet with an uppercase tab bar, fused composer, numbered ruled select list with a tick, dashed chips; the most complete control and frame system, though 17 small targets.
Ruled fields and caps SEND key are good, but the serif Finish setting head wraps awkwardly above the tab bar and 20 targets are under 44px.
Large two-line question, underlined fields and an arrowed chip row: the clearest title-action-content order and a strong rule set, though it is light on phosphor and has 41 small targets.
The old reference: tube with the question inside it is charming but the typed box sits in the glass and the composer is buried.

Folding the glass to one READY line puts the composer on the first screen, with slate plates and amber Finish setting up visible; the change shows across pages and costs only the hidden monitors until opened.
Head-1 plus a spend dial and light numerals; the Home shown is unchanged, so the gain sits on Status only.
Counted Folio with a faint runner; the visible Home difference is a status line already present, and the ground sits outside the signature band.
Squarer boxes and section caps are a minor tweak; the press afterglow is invisible in stills and Home reads as the parent.
Dated spine for To do serves the overdue task, the split-key select with a ticked list is a real control gain, and the small-caps labels add rhythm.
Counted ends add structure to heads, but the Home card is the parent's and tick marks mixed with numerals are an odd grammar.
Cream ink makes the Blueprint warmer, but the running head repeats the bar and title and adds height above the question.
The Blueprint's strong system with quiet head links; the pilot lamp and breathing are barely visible, the rest is sound.
Grid Console with a counted head and steel and pewter lamps instead of red and amber; calm, but the same serif wrap flaw at the foot and the lamp key adds words.
Bolder dial and dotted leaders help the Status page and ledger rows; Home is the parent's.
Serif Swiss heading with a short rule under the current tab: elegant and clear, but serif titles have faded before and the select key works only in Chromium.
Swiss Thread with a raised graphite select key, a raised Send and real small caps: clear controls and rhythm, a calm page, though the extra face and 41 small targets cost it.

The giant lit question and full-width Send make the one action unmissable, the tube light is restored and the numbered index is a coherent navigation idea; the length on a phone and the olive lit word are the costs.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the uppercase tab bar, fused composer and numbered ruled select list; enlarge the 17 sub-44px targets (chips, the checkbox row) and let the pilot lamp and phosphor halo show on the glass so the light is not only on the frame.

Keep the folded READY line and the slate plates; make it open on the Next up and radar when something is live or a plan is today, and use a slightly heavier weight for the light numerals so the dim rows read.

Keep the giant lit question, full-width Send and numbered index; cut the Home length on a phone by collapsing the index to count and one live line per row, brighten the green of the lit word so it does not read olive, and level the row heights.

Take the To do dated spine with the NOW lamp and the split-key select into a calmer parent; fix the tall rows and the Tab order, and make the small-caps labels larger so they do not fade beside the body face.
Keep the quiet head-link row and lit foot rule; make the pilot lamp sit on the glass beside the status line so the signal is seen where she answers.
Keep the strict grid and big question; return some bloom to the lit word and the Send key, and raise the 41 sub-44px targets.

judges.notes: On the phone, Home is judged by whether the eye goes title, then the composer, then the content. Swiss Thread and Lit Index do this best because the question is large and the action is full-width. The Blueprint does it best as a complete system: tab bar, fused composer, ruled select list and dashed chips would hold on Plans, To do and Settings. Folded Slate is the best new idea for use, since it brings the composer to the first screen and changes colour across the page. Most Desk Terminal, Track and Tallied children are near-identical on Home and change only a status line, a runner or a count, so they score low on the owner's nearly-identical test. The Grid Console family has a serif Finish setting heading that wraps badly above the tab bar. Lit Index brings back the most original tube light, which the owner asked for, but it costs length. Several designs have many targets under 44px, notably Swiss Thread at 41 and the Grid Console at 20.

parts.what: numbered ruled select list with a tick, fused composer row with square Send, dashed arrow chips
uppercase tab bar with a lit top edge on the current tab
one status line under the question (Listening, watching 4 plans) with a lit dot
one Vera card holding greeting, question, status line, composer and Send, with chips beneath
large two-line question with the one lit word, date on the right, composer straight below

scores.why: Near-monochrome green on black with flat cards; the light is only a few dots and the monitor, and nothing varies by page content.

Real layout change on every page (tube rail left, index list, keyed filters, big Add button) with cream ink and teal ground; the tube keeps genuine phosphor, though the rail is a heavy chunk and Settings is a plain list.

Serif titles with page-coloured counts, a dated spine with lit NOW and a clock dial change whole pages and ground the colour; but the serif loses some of the green-screen character and the glow is mostly on dots.
The spend gauge and scope are lovely light, but the rest is a grey, near-neutral table page with thin lamps; it reads as an editor theme outside the tubes.
Blueprint sheet frames, grid and numbered rows alter every page and keep sparks on the green, but the faint grid and pencil bands risk reading as a costume and the Status tube is lost below the fold.

The most atmospheric: a lit rule line with nodes through each page, serif titles, a big gauge and the NOW stamp, with bloom where the phosphor belongs; the Status head has a lot of empty black and the lines are faint.
Big sans titles and coloured rules on Settings are a clear typographic change, but the ground is grey-black, the phosphor nearly vanishes, and it reads as a generic dark dashboard.
The early Desk Terminal reference works as a bar: tube rail and tidy rows, but the blue-grey plates and mixed controls are plainer than the later keyed version.
Folding the tube to a READY line removes the monitors the owner likes and the radar, and the slate plates are the only real change; this is a regression of the parent's best feature.
Head-1 plus a moving-coil dial and bolder lead words adds a real glowing instrument on Status, but the other three pages are nearly identical to head-1.
Near duplicate of head-2; the alternate-row runner is almost invisible at normal viewing and the ground shift is imperceptible.
Near duplicate of head-2 with thin coloured caps and squarer corners; tasteful and slightly crisper, but a subtle change across the pages and the afterglow is invisible in stills.
The To do spine with dated margin and NOW lamp beside the scope is a good list change on that page, but the other pages are the grey head-3 and the rows are tall.
Ticks and end caps on the masthead are small gestures on a grey, matte page; the repeated count (title, ticks, strip) is noise.
Cream ink and a running head warm the blueprint, but the running head just repeats the bar and the title and the change from head-4 is small.
A pilot lamp in the footer and dotted head links barely change the blueprint; the headline signal cannot be seen.
Grid Console with a typed count on the rule and a foot pilot lamp is a pleasant, glowing frame, but the Status head gets a hollow void and the Up plate is decoration.
Grid Console with a larger lit dial and LIMIT flag, a halo on lead words and a lit rule thread keeps the tube's light where it belongs; the dotted leaders and the empty sector are hardly visible.
Serif headings on the Swiss grid soften it a little but cut against the green-screen feel, and the phosphor is nearly absent.
Keys, small caps and a cooler ground are tiny refinements on the Swiss page; a fourth typeface appears and little light remains.

The poster index with giant condensed titles and a single lit word changes every page's structure and type, the biggest departure; the lit green is olive in places, the glow only returns on the Status monitor, and the pages run long.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the lit thread through each page with node markers, the NOW stamp, and the gauge. Fix the dead black above the Status head and make the line and tray corners slightly brighter so they do not vanish on a dim display.

Keep the larger lit dial, the lead-word halo and the thread. Make the dotted leaders and the fill visible at normal size, and give Settings and To do one more change so the work is not confined to Status.

Keep the huge condensed titles, the folio and the lit word. Brighten the lit word so it is phosphor and not olive, trim the index to shorter pages, and put the tube's bloom on one more place than the Status monitor.

Keep the serif title with its counted readout and the dated spine. Add more phosphor halo to the NOW node and the count so the page does not read as only a book, and give Settings the same spine logic.
The keyed rail and lit tube work. Shrink the rail on the Status page, since it crowds the content, and lift Settings out of the plain list.
Fold only when the tube has nothing to say. Keep the radar, spend and Next up visible by default, since those are the motif.
Keep the gauge and scope. Warm up the grey ground and bring a lamp-glow to the table lamps so the page outside the tubes is not an editor theme.

judges.notes: The field has three real families (tube rail, Grid Console with a lit thread, Blueprint) plus wild-1's poster and a cluster of near duplicates that differ by a footer lamp, a runner or a rounding step. Those small mutants should score low on the owner's test. The strongest designs bring the tube's light to the page content (a lit thread, the NOW stamp, a dial) while using grounded material elsewhere. Grey-ground designs (head-3, Swiss) lose the signature, and the Blueprint risks costume. The owner's latest word asked to bring back the light, so the Grid Console line and the dial deserve most development; wild-1 is the only genuinely new structure and merits another round to fix its olive lit word.
